MINUTES OF THE AFTERNOON SESSION
FRIDAY, JUNE 16. 1944
Seaview Country Club
Absecon. New Jersey
THE
annual Convention, held in the 111th year of the Psi Upsilon
Fraternity, under the auspices of the Executive Council, was called
to order at 3 :03 P.M. at the Seaview Country Club. Absecon. New Jersey,
by Scott Turner, Phi '02. President of the Executive Council, who, after
welcoming the delegates, appointed Stephen G. Kent. Delta Delta '11.
Secretary of the Executive Council, as Temporary Recorder, Ralph F.
Khuen. Phi '15. as Temporary First Assistant Recorder, and Jerome W.
Brush. Jr., Delta Delta '39. as Temporary Second Assistant Recorder.
Brother Turner then appointed the following committees, by customary
rotation :
On Credentials:
J. J. E. Hessey. Nu '13, Chairman
Charles H. Blair, Chi '97
R. McClelland Brady, Beta Beta '90
A. E. Forstall, Eta '83

S. L. Rosenberry, Rho '23. Chairman
George T. Sharp, Tan '11
A. Northey Jones, Beta Beta '17
Eugene Vinet, Epsilon Phi '11
A motion was duly adopted that the Convention take a recess of ten
minutes to enable the committees to prepare reports.
At the end of the recess, Brother Turner called the Convention to
order.

The Annual Communication of the Executive Council was read by
Benjamin T. Burton. Chi '21, Vice-President of the Executive Council.
At the conclusion of the reading, all present stood for one minute with
bowed heads in honor of the Brothers who have given their lives for their
country.
A motion was adopted that this Communication be accepted, placed on
file, and referred to the Committee on Annual Communications.
The Committee on Credentials rendered a supplementary report that

RECORDS OF THE CONVENTION
A. Northey Jones. Beta Beta '17. Treasurer of the Executive Council.
read the annual Treasurer's Report, copies of which were passed to the
delegates.
A motion was adopted that the Treasurer's Report be accepted with a
vote of appreciation to the Treasurer, and that such report be placed on file
and referred to the Committee on Annual Communications.
The President then called for oral reports from the Chapters, which
were rendered as follows :
TflETA�
There are eight undergraduate active members and four
pledges.' The Chapter initiated four Brothers in December and two in
April. Meetings are held every two weeks. Finances are in good shape.
The Chapter House is occupied by 70 men in the Naval V-12 unit at
Union.
Delta�
Brother Thomas Rickenback. '46, is the sole undergraduate.
but a number of alumni have become active members. An attempt will be
I made to pledge and initiate more members. The lease of the House to the
University will terminate in July, but finances are in good shape.
Sigma�
The fraternity situation at Brown was summarized. Psi Upsi
lon is one of five fraternities which, thus far, have declined to deed their
properties to the University. The Sigma has fourteen undergraduate active
members on the campus, and is in a strong financial position.
A motion was thereupon adopted that the Sigma's problem be referred
for consideration to the Committee on New Business.
Oral reports were then continued as follows :
Gamma�
The Gamma at present has no undergraduate active mem
bers ; its financial position is sound.
Zeta�
There have been no new developments during the last year.
At 4 :45, the Convention recessed until 5 :1S, to enable the Alumni
Association to hold its annual meeting. President Turner again took the
chair at 5 :1S.
Lambda�
The Chapter is not operating ; its future prospects at Colum
bia are hard to predict.
Kappa�The Kappa still has four undergraduate members in college.
No meetings have been held other than initiatory. Only fifty civilian under
graduates remain in College. The House is being used by the College as
a dormitory and club house for the radar Navy unit.
Psi�
No undergraduate members remain on the campus. Some alumni
members will become active on June 24, 1944. A small amount of revenue
has been received from the rent of the House.
Xi�
The Xi is still functioning as normally as possible. (According to
last reports it numbers eight undergraduate members and four pledges.)
Pledging and initiation of new men continue.

Upsilon�
The present situation is fully covered by the Chapter letter
in the June issue of The Diamond.
Iota�
^The Chapter continues its traditional lodge procedure; it has
vitality, and will successfully meet its future problems.
Phi�
The Chapter has fifteen active student members. The House is
being used by the University as a freshman dormitory; the rental is $280
monthly. Initiation was held at Brother Khuen's house in Detroit.
Omega�
Four undergraduate members remain on the campus. Meetings
are being held regularly, with alumni active members present. Finances are
excellent.
Pi�
The Chapter is still first on the campus. Finances are excellent,
the Chapter House, however, is being used as a barracks.
The Committee on Credentials reported that J. Lee Grunst, '46, a dele
gate of Epsilon Nu, was present, and that his credentials were in order, and
that George W. Blabon, Tau '22, (not a delegate) was also in attendance.
After the acceptance of this report, oral reports of the Chapters were
continued as follows :
Chi�
The Chapter is not functioning. The House has been taken over
by the University for the use of the Navy. Finances are in good shape.
Ten student members remain at Ithaca. They hold informal social gather
ings, but no formal meetings.
Beta Beta�
There has been no pledging or initiating for over a year.
One undergraduate member remains at Trinity. No alumni have become
active members. The financial situation is satisfactory.
Eta�
The Chapter is not functioning. Finances are in sound condition.
The University owns the House, but the Chapter has a favorable contract
for its occupancy. During the last year, the University has made use of
the House and it has been kept in excellent condition. About one year's
rent is still due to the Chapter.
Tau�
The Chapter has eleven active undergraduates, of whom eight are
in service. There are also eight active alumni members. Two undergrad
uates will leave in June. Rushing continues, and two initiations have been
held this year. Finances are satisfactory.
At 7 :10 P.M. a motion was adopted that the Convention take a recess,
to reconvene immediately following dinner.
MINUTES OF THE EVENING SESSION

Seaview Country Club

Appendix A
THE ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
OF THE
EXECUTIVE COUNCIL
TO THE
1944 CONVENTION OF PSI UPSILON
HELD UNDER THE AUSPICES OF THE
EXECUTIVE COUNCIL
Absecon, New Jersby
June 16. 1944
The Executive Council is acting as host to this 102nd Convention held
in the 111th Year of our Fraternity. The Council cordially welcomes, and
extends a true Psi Upsilon greeting to, each delegate of our twenty-eight
chapters and each other brother present. Your loyalty and your interest
in Psi Upsilon which makes this Convention possible in this war year is
indeed gratifying.
Chapter Visits :
Difficulties of travel, as well as conditions prevailing at the educational
institutions where our chapters are situated, have made it impossible for
the Executive Council to maintain its usual schedule of chapter visits.
Nevertheless, members of the Council or their representatives have made
personal visits since our last Convention to the following chapters : Iota.
Gamma, Omicron, Lambda. Nu and Eta.
In addition, by correspondence and in some cases by long distance tele
phone, informal reports on the condition of all the other chapters have been
obtained.
Condition of Frateknity:
Our three Canadian chapters and the following chapters located in the
United States�
Theta, Delta, Sigma, Kappa. Xi, Upsilon, Iota. Phi, Omega.
Tau, Rho. Epsilon. Theta Theta. and Epsilon Nu still maintain an under
graduate membership and, to the extent still feasible, carry on the activities
of a fraternity chapter. The Upsilon, however, has just announced that it
plans to suspend the pledging of new members.
At our other chapters, our latest information is that either no under
graduate members remain on the campus, or that they do not contemplate
pledging or initiating new members until the termination of war conditions.
Page Fourteen

PSI UPSILON FRATERNITY
Nevertheless, as suggested by the Executive Council, in most of our
chapters which lack an undergraduate membership a limited number of
alumni have become active members, thus keeping alive an organization
through which new members may be pledged and initiated at the earliest
possible moment. It is hoped that all chapters will adopt this procedure.
In making the foregoing recommendation, the Executive Council wishes
to emphasize that its purpose is not to create revenue for the national
fraternity. Pursuant to our Constitution and resolutions adopted in Con
ventions, for each active member each chapter is required to pay to the
national fraternity annual taxes and assessments aggregating $4.00, of
which $1.00 goes into the fund out of which appropriations are made to
chapters for Convention purposes. Feeling that this requirement might
obstruct the attainment of its objective, at its meeting held January 11,
1944. the Executive Council determined that it tentatively would hill each
chapter a maximum amount of $20.00 for all of its alumni who are active
members regardless of their number ; that this practice be continued
throughout the period of the war; and that ratification and approval
of this course of action be sought from this Convention. We believe that
such procedure is in the interest of the Fraternity and we respectfully
request formal action on your part to authorize and approve it. including
the adoption of an appropriate amendment to our Constitution.
At a great many of the colleges and universities where we have chapters
there existed prior to the war rather detailed and complicatd rushing
rules. Many of such rules are likely to prove obstacles to the prompt
revival of the fraternities under the conditions first prevailing following
the cessation of hostilities in Europe and in Japan. This is a subject which
alumni organizations of chapters might well study with the object of
arranging a temporary modification of these rushing rules through alumni
interfraternity committees, to the end that all fraternities on the particular
campus may at the earliest practical moment regain an undergraduate active
membership.
In most of our chapters, alumni organizations have taken intelligent
and vigorous steps to conserve chapter properties and to avoid creation of
additional financial burdens as a result of the war conditions. It is hoped
that these efforts will be continued and broadened, and that each chapter
will find a way to overcome all financial difficulties. Our Committee on
War Problems stands ready at any time to offer to any chapter such sug
gestions as experience elsewhere has proven effective.
In addition, through its Committee on War Problems, the Executive
Council has been giving study to ways and means of rendering member
ship in Psi Upsilon more worthwhile to our younger brothers in the post
war period, to the end that not only our traditional ties of friendship
between members may be fostered and strengthened, but that more than
ever before in its long history Psi Upsilon may prove a constructive force
Page Fifteen

PSI UPSILON FRATERNITY
in building a capacity for leadership and a high spirit of citizenship in
those who join our ranks. The National Interfraternity Conference, of
which we continue to be a member, is also devoting much time and atten
tion to these same objectives, and we are receiving from time to time the
benefit of such suggestions as the Conference makes.
Sigma Chapter:
The administration at Brown University has been endeavoring to bring
about radical changes in the housing of fraternities with the apparent ob
jective of eventually locating all fraternities in dormitories on the campus.
The plan contemplates that each fraternity would deed its present property
as a gift to the University. The proposal seems to have impressed the
alumni of several fraternities as advantageous. On the other hand, the
alumni of other fraternities (including our Sigma Chapter, which owns a
substantial house free of mortgage indebtedness) desire to continue to own
and operate their own fraternity houses and have a preference for an offcampus site. The alumni of our Sigma Chapter are being subjected to
pressure from those desiring an outcome favorable to their own interests,
and there are numerous cross-currents of local opinion. Under these cir
cumstances, the Trustees of our Sigma Chapter's alumni corporation have
been devoting time and attention to seeking a solution which will not
involve uncompensated sacrifice of present assets, and which will assure
the Sigma every prospect of remaining a strong chapter of Psi Upsilon.
New Federal Tax Law:
Your attention is called to the fact that, under the Federal Revenue
Act of 1943, an annual income tax return will be required from the
national fraternity, The Psi Upsilon Alumni Association, each under
graduate chapter, each alumni organization, and each local alumni Psi
Upsilon club. This does not mean that any tax is to be paid, but merely
that a return must be filed. The federal tax authorities have indicated
that forms of returns will be available about June 15, 1944. and that they
must be filed on or before August 15. 1944. Definite regulations have
not yet been issued, and the filing date may be changed. This is a matter
as to which all should be on the alert, as failure to file may involve sub
stantial money penalties. The Executive Council plans to make available
to you such further information on this subject as it ascertains.
The Diamond:
Brother Jerome W. Brush, Jr., Delta Delta '39, was compelled to resign
as editor of the Diamond. We were fortunate in obtaining the services of
Edward C. Peattie, Phi '06, as editor during the current year. He has

adopted last year. Much emphasis has been placed on the news of war

activities of our members. We believe that receiving the Diamond means
much to our younger brothers in active service. In order that its value to
them may be increased, the cooperation of every alumnus is asked in for

of brothers in the armed forces. The Fraternity is indeed indebted to
Brother Peattie for his unselfish and generous contribution of time as editor
of the Diamond.
Psi Upsilon Jewelry:
Army and Navy regulations preclude the wearing of pins by members
of the armed forces. Rings, however, are permitted. Under these circum
stances, believing that our brothers in service should have some means of
identifying each other, the Executive Council has had designed a Psi
Upsilon ring to be worn only by members in service. Rings may be ob
tained at a cost ranging from $4 to $14 per ring by making application
at our headquarters office. We ask your ratification of this arrangement
and your approval of its continuance.

General:
In these days, we of the older generation feel most humble in speaking
of our younger brothers. In common with others of their age. they have
been called upon to obliterate evils which they did not create and to risk
their all to build a better future. The magnificent spirit with which they
are meeting this challenge makes one proud of them and of the nation
Page Eighteen

PSI UPSILON FRATERNITY
from which they sprang. The addition of each name to the list of those
who have made the final gift of life itself brings sadness. We are con
fident that each of our younger brothers will have the courage and deter
mination to see through to the end such tasks as are assigned to him,
and we devoutly pray that casualties among them will be very few. We
hope to see them safe and sound in our gatherings in the happier years of
future peace. We know that they will bring to us fresh energy and a new
sense of direction in building the future of Psi Upsilon.
This future must be constructed at a time when the fundamental
principles on which our government rests as well as its relationships with
other nations seem rapidly to shift before our very eyes. In short, we face
many years in which the solutions to a rapid succession of important
problems will have far-reaching consequences upon our own and succeeding
generations. Desirable results can best be achieved if the combined knowl
edge and experience of the nation is enlisted in the solution of these
problems.
Thus college fraternities face their greatest opportunity for usefulness
in the educational system and in the life of the nation. Fraternities owe
their origin
�
to the literary society. Psi Upsilon carries on the tradition
of the literary meeting. In the years ahead, let us have a great many more
of these discussion meetings and let these discussions center around the
nation's problems as one by one they arise.
Through members of fraternities and their families can be reached a
substantial cross-section of the thinking people of America. If enough
of them acquire understanding of, and devote time and study to. the
nation's difficulties, out of the combined intelligence and experience of all
will arise programs which will merit and will receive united support.
May Psi Upsilon make an important contribution toward bringing about
such a result.
If ever there was a time when our country and this Fraternity needed
leadership and clear thinking, it is today. Those of us who love Psi
Upsilon must strive to preserve and protect her.
O, dear old shrine
Our hearts around thee twine
We love thee yet
We'll ne'er forget
The days of Auld Lang Syne.
The Committee of the Executive Council of Psi Upsilon,
ON the Annual Communication to the 1944 Convention.

EXECUTIVE COUNCIL OF PSI UPSILON FRATERNITY
Report of the Treasurer
1944
There is presented herewith a statement of the net worth of the
various funds of the Fraternity held by the Executive Council as of April
30, 1944, a summary of income and expenses of the various funds for the
year ended April 30, 1944, and certain comparative figures for the year
ended April 30, 1943. A list of investments held in the General Fund.
the Bridgman Fund, the Douglas Fund and the Diamond Life Subscription
Fund is also presented.
Generally speaking, the results of the year ended April 30. 1944 may
be considered very satisfactory, as the net worth of the various funds of
the Fraternity increased over $3,000 during the year after allocating the
total amount received for Diamond life subscriptions, viz.. $2,335, to the
reserve for Diamond life subscriptions. That we were able to do as well
as we did despite war-time conditions and the relatively small number of
men in the chapters was largely due to the fact that we received a bequest
of $2,000 from Archibald Douglas. Lambda '94, a past President of the
Executive Council, and fifty copies of the Annals of Psi Upsilon, valued
at $175, from Mrs. Standish Backus, and that we realized a profit of
something over $2,000 on the sale of securities. These gifts and profits
more than offset such operating losses as were experienced. The Fraternity
is very grateful for these gifts. Brother Douglas stipulated that his gift
should be used towards the publication of the Diamond, and in accordance
with his wishes the $2,000 has been placed in a fund known as the Douglas
Fund, the interest on which will be used, and the principal if necessary,
to maintain its publication.
The cash position of the Fraternity has improved since April 30 by
the collection of $287 of chapter taxes and $465 for Diamond life sub
scriptions. Accounts receivable on June 15,- 1944, therefore amounted to
$769 due from six chapters. While this is a better situation than existed
a year ago at Convention time, it is not up to our usual record prior to
the war of having all chapter taxes and Diamond life subscriptions paid
before the Convention. The situation with respect to our investments is
the best that it has been since our Centennial in 1933. We have securities
which cost us $53,526 and which on April 30. 1944 had a market value
of �53.712, a value slightly in excess of the cost�
and this is after taking
$2,036 of profits on security sales during the year.

RECORDS OF THE CONVENTIOM
We had a slight loss on operations in the General Fund this past year
compared with a slight profit in 1943. The loss on publishing the Diamond
was $766 this year, in comparison with a loss of $1,682 in 1943. The
Executive Council has replenished the current Diamond fund by a transfer
of $1,000 from the Convention Fund, and this Convention will be asked
to pass a resolution ratifying such transfer. Our reserve for Diamond life
subscriptions accumulated in the past five years now amounts to $26,142,
and is invested as shown in the statement. The policy of setting up
Diamond life subscription moneys in a reserve rather than of spending
such subscription moneys to meet the current running expenses of the
Diamond is a vast improvement over the practice prior to five years ago
when no such reserve was set up. It is expected that the Diamond Life
Subscription Fund will be gradually built up by the $15 payments for life
subscriptions so that the publication costs of the Diamond can eventually
be met in a businesslike manner from annuity payments from the Fund.
The 4% annuity payment from the Fund in this past year amounted to $953.
The Secretary and Treasurer of the Fraternity are Trustees of the
Willard Fiske Fund, the assets of which are not shown in the attached
statement. This fund is being kept intact until it reaches $1,000. It now
amounts to approximately $683, consisting of United States Government
Series F bonds due November 1954. with a present redemption value of
$668, and $15 in a savings bank account.
Again the Treasurer wishes to reiterate that every effort is being
made to keep expenses, and consequently chapter taxes, at a minimum.
Taxes of $4 per man per year are low in comparison with taxes of other
fraternities. The Treasurer takes this opportunity to thank the Treasurers
of the Chapters for their cooperation in these difficult war-time days.
Respectfully submitted,
Allen Northey Jones,
Treasurer.
June 16, 1944
